items.readable_text:
Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c671f7e960b080ea89d2639fc94d768a]

Content:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as

Content:
[MATH: x=t^3-1, \qquad
y=2t-t^3, \qquad
t \in (-\infty, \infty).]

Content:
The shaded area shown in the diagram is the finite region bounded between the curve, the [MATH: x]-axis, and the vertical lines formed by [MATH: x]-axis and the points on the curve corresponding to [MATH: t_1=0] to [MATH: t_2=1,] as shown.

Content:
We know that the area of the curve is given by

Content:
[MATH: A = \int_{a}^{b} y \:\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
Since our curve is defined parametrically, we need to change the variable of integration from [MATH: x] to [MATH: t] using the change of variables formula, given by

Content:
[MATH: A = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y(t) \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm d t}\:\textrm d t.]

Content:
Now, in this case, we have

Content:
[MATH: (dx)/(dt) = (d)/(dt)(t^{3} − 1) = 3t^{2}.]

Content:
Applying the change of variables formula, we have

Content:
[MATH: A|= ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y(t)(dx)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}(2t − t^{3}) ⋅ 3t^{2}dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}6t^{3} − 3t^{5}dt; = 6∫_{0}^{1}t^{3}dt − 3∫_{0}^{1}t^{5}dt; = 6 ⋅ (t^{4})/(4)|_{0}^{1} − 3 ⋅ (t^{6})/(6)|_{0}^{1}; = 6((1)/(4) − 0) − 3((1)/(6) − 0); = (3)/(2) − (1)/(2); = 1.]

Content:
Therefore, the shaded area shown in the picture has an area of [MATH: 1] square unit.

sections.normalized_html: In general, the area between the [MATH: x]-axis and the parametric curve [MATH: x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2]

sections.normalized_html: is given by the absolute value of the integral

sections.normalized_html: [MATH: \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.]
sections.readable_text: [MATH: \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.]

sections.normalized_html: Note the following:
sections.readable_text: Note the following:

sections.normalized_html:
• When applying this formula, we assume that the chosen parametrization traverses the curve only once.

  • It's possible that this integral gives a negative value for the area even when the corresponding region lies entirely above the [MATH: x]-axis!

    To see why, note that if the curve lies above the [MATH: x]-axis, we must have [MATH: y(t) > 0.] However, if the curve is parameterized so that it is traversed from right to left, then [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0,] and we have [MATH: y\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0] and thus, our integral turns out to be negative.

  • To ensure that we get an unsigned area, we take the absolute value of the integral.

  • In general, care must be taken when asked to compute the area bounded by a parametric curve when [MATH: y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}] changes sign over the domain of integration. However, we won't consider that scenario here.

Content:
In general, the area between the [MATH: x]-axis and the parametric curve
[MATH: x = x(t), \qquad
y = y(t), \qquad
t_1 \leq t \leq t_2]

Content:
is given by the absolute value of the integral

Content:
[MATH: \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- When applying this formula, we assume that the chosen parametrization traverses the curve only once.
- It's possible that this integral gives a negative value for the area even when the corresponding region lies entirely above the [MATH: x]-axis!

To see why, note that if the curve lies above the [MATH: x]-axis, we must have [MATH: y(t) > 0.] However, if the curve is parameterized so that it is traversed from right to left, then [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0,] and we have
[MATH: y\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0]
and thus, our integral turns out to be negative.
- To ensure that we get an unsigned area, we take the absolute value of the integral.
- In general, care must be taken when asked to compute the area bounded by a parametric curve when [MATH: y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}] changes sign over the domain of integration. However, we won't consider that scenario here.

sections.normalized_html: Find an integral expression for the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as [MATH: x = e^{-t^2}, \qquad y = t^3,] and the [MATH: x]-axis for [MATH: 0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{2} \,?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/c513f83df573aeab8a8c09f8f0a6946f]

Find an integral expression for the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as
[MATH: x = e^{-t^2}, \qquad y = t^3,]
and the [MATH: x]-axis for [MATH: 0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{2} \,?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve [MATH: x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2]

and the [MATH: x]-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

[MATH: \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.]

First, we compute

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(e^{− t^{2}}); = − 2te^{− t^{2}}.]

So, we obtain the integral expression [MATH: ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y(dx)/(dt)dt|= ∫_{0}^{sqrt(2)}t^{3}(− 2te^{− t^{2}})dt; = − 2∫_{0}^{sqrt(2)}t^{4}e^{− t^{2}}dt.]

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since [MATH: y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \leq 0] for all [MATH: t \in [0, \sqrt{2}].]

Therefore, the area is given by [MATH: A = -\left( -2 \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} t^4 e^{-t^2} \, \textrm{d}t \right) = 2 \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} t^4 e^{-t^2} \, \textrm{d}t.]

[MATH: x = t^2 - 1, \qquad y = t^3 - 4t]
and the [MATH: x]-axis for [MATH: t \in [-2,0].]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve [MATH: x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2]

and the [MATH: x]-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

[MATH: \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.]

First, we compute

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(t^{2} − 1); = 2t.]

So, we obtain the integral expression [MATH: ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y(dx)/(dt)dt|= ∫_{− 2}^{0}(t^{3} − 4t)(2t)dt; = 2∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{2}(t^{2} − 4)dt.]

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since [MATH: y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \leq 0] for all [MATH: t \in [-2,0].]

Therefore, the area is [MATH: A|= − 2∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{2}(t^{2} − 4)dt; = 2∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{2}(4 − t^{2})dt; = 2∫_{− 2}^{0}(4t^{2} − t^{4})dt; = 8∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{2}dt − 2∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{4}dt; = 8 ⋅ (t^{3})/(3)|_{− 2}^{0} − 2 ⋅ (t^{5})/(5)|_{− 2}^{0}; = 8((0^{3})/(3) − ((− 2)^{3})/(3)) − 2((0^{5})/(5) − ((− 2)^{5})/(5)); = 8((8)/(3)) − 2((32)/(5)); = (64)/(3) − (64)/(5); = (128)/(15).]

[MATH: \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- When applying this formula, we assume that the chosen parametrization traverses the curve only once.
- It's possible that this integral gives a negative value for the area even when the corresponding region lies entirely above the [MATH: x]-axis!

To see why, note that if the curve lies above the [MATH: x]-axis, we must have [MATH: y(t) > 0.] However, if the curve is parameterized so that it is traversed from right to left, then [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0,] and we have
[MATH: y\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0]
and thus, our integral turns out to be negative.
- To ensure that we get an unsigned area, we take the absolute value of the integral.
- In general, care must be taken when asked to compute the area bounded by a parametric curve when [MATH: y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}] changes sign over the domain of integration. However, we won't consider that scenario here.

Item 3 — Example: Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/c513f83df573aeab8a8c09f8f0a6946f]

Find an integral expression for the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as
[MATH: x = e^{-t^2}, \qquad y = t^3,]
and the [MATH: x]-axis for [MATH: 0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{2} \,?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve
[MATH: x = x(t), \qquad
y = y(t), \qquad
t_1 \leq t \leq t_2]

and the [MATH: x]-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

[MATH: \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.]

First, we compute

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(e^{− t^{2}}); = − 2te^{− t^{2}}.]

So, we obtain the integral expression
[MATH: ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y(dx)/(dt)dt|= ∫_{0}^{sqrt(2)}t^{3}(− 2te^{− t^{2}})dt; = − 2∫_{0}^{sqrt(2)}t^{4}e^{− t^{2}}dt.]

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since [MATH: y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \leq 0] for all [MATH: t \in [0, \sqrt{2}].]

Therefore, the area is given by
[MATH: A = -\left( -2 \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} t^4 e^{-t^2} \, \textrm{d}t \right) = 2 \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} t^4 e^{-t^2} \, \textrm{d}t.]

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/dfb51044c9a617346fc91c88a9c92939]

Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as
[MATH: x = t^2 - 1, \qquad y = t^3 - 4t]
and the [MATH: x]-axis for [MATH: t \in [-2,0].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve
[MATH: x = x(t), \qquad
y = y(t), \qquad
t_1 \leq t \leq t_2]

and the [MATH: x]-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

[MATH: \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.]

First, we compute

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(t^{2} − 1); = 2t.]

So, we obtain the integral expression
[MATH: ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y(dx)/(dt)dt|= ∫_{− 2}^{0}(t^{3} − 4t)(2t)dt; = 2∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{2}(t^{2} − 4)dt.]

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since [MATH: y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \leq 0] for all [MATH: t \in [-2,0].]

Therefore, the area is
[MATH: A|= − 2∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{2}(t^{2} − 4)dt; = 2∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{2}(4 − t^{2})dt; = 2∫_{− 2}^{0}(4t^{2} − t^{4})dt; = 8∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{2}dt − 2∫_{− 2}^{0}t^{4}dt; = 8 ⋅ (t^{3})/(3)|_{− 2}^{0} − 2 ⋅ (t^{5})/(5)|_{− 2}^{0}; = 8((0^{3})/(3) − ((− 2)^{3})/(3)) − 2((0^{5})/(5) − ((− 2)^{5})/(5)); = 8((8)/(3)) − 2((32)/(5)); = (64)/(3) − (64)/(5); = (128)/(15).]
